# SolarCon: Adaptive, drift-compensated MPPT and supervisory control of a PV–battery DC bus

*Technical report — computational study, averaged models. All results generated by
`scripts/run_experiments.py`; complete tables in `results/metrics/tables.md`.*

## 1. Problem

A 4.8 kW PV array (24 × Kyocera KC200GT, 8s×3p) feeds a 400 V DC bus through a boost
converter; a 40 Ah, ≈300 V battery is interfaced through a synchronous bidirectional buck–boost
converter; a constant-power load is connected to the bus. The controller must (i) extract maximum
PV power under changing irradiance, temperature and shading, (ii) hold the bus at 400 V, and
(iii) respect battery SOC, current and voltage limits, curtailing PV or shedding load only when
the battery cannot absorb or supply the imbalance.

## 2. Models

* **PV:** single-diode model; `a = 1.3`, `Rs`, `Rsh` extracted from the datasheet MPP with the
  `dP/dV = 0` condition; explicit Lambert-W current evaluated with the Wright-omega function;
  `I0(T)` chosen so Voc follows the datasheet `Kv`. Partial shading: per-module bypass diodes,
  tabulated string curve.
* **Converters:** state-space averaged CCM models (boost with optional conduction/diode/switching
  losses; synchronous bidirectional half-bridge).
* **Battery:** first-order Thevenin model with a synthetic NMC-like OCV curve.
* **Integration:** RK4 at the 50 µs control period with ZOH duty cycles.

Equations and parameter values: `docs/model_equations.md`, `docs/design_assumptions.md`.

**Validation of the PV model.** The extracted model reproduces the STC datasheet point
(Pmax 200.1 W, +0.07 %). The datasheet NOCT row (800 W/m², 47 °C) was **not** used for fitting
and serves as an independent check: Pmax 142.2 W vs 142 W (+0.14 %), Isc +0.06 %, Voc −0.47 %,
Vmp +1.2 %, Imp −1.2 %. Unit tests also verify the residual of the implicit equation
(< 1e-8 A), the V(I)/I(V) inverse pair, and finiteness for voltages far beyond Voc.

## 3. Control architecture

Cascaded PI loops with feed-forward, duty saturation mapped onto the PI output limits, and
back-calculation anti-windup:

* PV side: MPPT → `v_ref` → voltage loop (200 Hz) → inductor-current loop (1.5 kHz) → `d`.
* Battery side: bus-voltage loop (40 Hz, with bus-current feed-forward) → `i_b,ref` limited by the
  EMS → battery-current loop (1 kHz) → `d_b`.
* Supervisor (DC-bus signalling): exactly one bus-forming loop at a time. Battery regulates
  400 V. If its charge current saturates, the bus rises to 410 V, where a PI loop shifts the PV
  reference to the right of the MPP (curtailment, MPPT frozen). If its discharge current
  saturates, the bus falls to 390 V, where a PI loop sheds load. SOC limits act through current
  limits derated to zero over the last 2 % SOC, so mode transitions are continuous.

## 4. MPPT methods and fair tuning

* **P&O** and **IncCond** (fixed step).
* **dP-P&O** (Sera et al., 2006): a mid-period power sample cancels a linear irradiance trend,
  removing the drift of P&O during ramps.
* **Adaptive dP-P&O (proposed):** dP-P&O decision plus variable step
  `ΔV = clip(M |dP| / ΔV_prev, ΔV_min, ΔV_max)`.
* **+ scan:** a 12-point reference sweep triggered by a > 15 % power change, for partial shading.

All trackers receive the same measurement (average of the last quarter of each MPPT period).
The four local trackers were tuned by the same grid search (12–48 parameter sets each) on three
training episodes that are not used for evaluation: a seeded random step/ramp irradiance profile,
the same profile with 0.5 % FS noise, and a cold start at 60 °C. Selected parameters:

| Method | Parameters | Mean training η |
|---|---|---|
| P&O | ΔV = 4 V, T_p = 5 ms | 99.45 % |
| IncCond | ΔV = 4 V, T_p = 5 ms, ε = 0 | 99.50 % |
| dP-P&O | ΔV = 4 V, T_p = 5 ms | 99.40 % |
| Adaptive dP-P&O | M = 0.1, ΔV ∈ [1, 8] V, T_p = 5 ms | 99.66 % |

An earlier tuning run that used only a noise-free episode starting near the MPP selected a very
small adaptive gain (M = 0.01), which made the adaptive tracker slow at cold start (η 98.4 % at
65 °C). Adding the cold-start and noisy episodes to the objective corrected this; the change is
documented here because the choice of tuning episodes visibly shapes the "optimised" controller.

## 5. Results

### 5.1 Tracking (ideal converters)

| Test | P&O | IncCond | dP-P&O | Adaptive dP-P&O |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A: η, STC | 99.84 % | 99.84 % | 99.84 % | 99.99 % |
| A: v_pv oscillation p-p | 8.7 V | 8.7 V | 8.7 V | 2.2 V |
| A: start-up from Voc to ±1 % P_mpp | 36 ms | 36 ms | 36 ms | 31 ms |
| B: η, irradiance steps | 99.83 % | 99.84 % | 99.83 % | 99.96 % |
| C: η, 15–65 °C at 1000 W/m² | 99.80–99.86 % | 99.80–99.93 % | 99.80–99.86 % | 99.99 % |
| C: η, 200–1000 W/m² at 25 °C | 99.83–99.85 % | 99.83–99.85 % | 99.83–99.85 % | 99.99 % |
| D: η, ramp down −350 W/m²/s | 99.91 % | 99.91 % | 99.82 % | 99.99 % |
| D: η, ramp up +1400 W/m²/s | 99.06 % | 99.10 % | 99.84 % | 99.99 % |

After the irradiance steps in B, the fixed-step trackers re-enter the ±1 % power band within
0–21 ms, but never satisfy the joint ±1 % power / ±2 % voltage settling criterion because their
steady oscillation (±4.3 V around a ≈ 210 V MPP) is wider than the voltage band; the adaptive
tracker settles in 6–51 ms. The ablation isolates the two mechanisms: drift compensation alone
(dP-P&O) fixes the ramp-up loss (99.06 → 99.84 %), and the adaptive step adds the reduction of
steady oscillation.

### 5.2 Partial shading (experiment E)

| | P&O | IncCond | dP-P&O | Adaptive | Adaptive + scan |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| η, pattern 1 (3 modules at 30 %) | 54.8 % | 54.8 % | 54.8 % | 55.0 % | 98.6 % |
| η, pattern 2 (two shading levels) | 70.4 % | 70.4 % | 70.4 % | 70.6 % | 98.9 % |

All local methods follow the operating point to the high-voltage local maximum; the scan
(triggered twice) finds the global maximum at ≈ 130 V for pattern 1. The scan costs about 12
MPPT periods (60 ms) of reduced power each time it fires and also fires on large uniform steps.

### 5.3 Robustness (experiment I)

Eight plants with L, Cin, C_dc ±20 %, battery R0 ±30 %, Q ±10 %, PV Rs/Rsh ±10 % (uniform), and
Gaussian measurement noise of 0.5 % of full scale on all six sensed quantities, profile B:

| | P&O | IncCond | dP-P&O | Adaptive dP-P&O |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| mean η | 99.76 % | 99.76 % | 99.63 % | 99.70 % |
| worst η | 99.74 % | 99.75 % | 99.56 % | 99.62 % |

Under noise the ranking reverses: the dP estimate `2P_x − P_k − P_{k+1}` combines three noisy power samples, so for
independent sample noise its variance is 3× that of the plain two-sample P&O difference, and wrong decisions near
the MPP cost more energy than the drift they prevent at these noise levels. Longer averaging
windows or a noise-adaptive dead band would be the next step.

### 5.4 DC bus, battery and supervisory control (experiments F, G, H)

* **H, load steps** 1→6→0.5→3 kW: maximum bus deviation 0.78 V with bus-current feed-forward;
  20.9 V and ≤ 146 ms settling to ±1 V with the PI loop alone (ablation). Lossy boost: 98.66 %
  modeled converter efficiency at STC; bus behaviour unchanged.
* **F:** the battery current changes sign with PV availability (charging ≈ 6 A at 1000 W/m²,
  discharging ≈ 6 A at 300 W/m², ≈ 10 A with no PV); PV_OFF is entered 0.1 s after PV power
  vanishes; bus within −0.81/+0.43 V.
* **G1:** at 88.8 % SOC the charge limit is derated to 12 A. When the load drops to zero the
  battery saturates, the bus overshoots to 421 V and the curtailment loop then holds 410 V
  (0.37 Wh curtailed in 1.5 s, ≈ 0.9 kW). No current or SOC violations.
* **G2:** at 10.5 % SOC the discharge limit is 10 A. When the load rises to 6 kW the bus falls
  to 385.5 V and load shedding holds 390 V (≈ 1.8 kW shed, 0.51 Wh in 1 s); full load is restored
  when demand drops to 2 kW.

### 5.5 Computational cost

100 simulations (250 s simulated) run in about 3 minutes on 2 CPU cores; the coupled model
needs 0.9–1.4 s of wall time per simulated second per core in pure Python. Per-run runtimes are in the metrics CSVs.

## 6. Limitations and extensions

Averaged CCM models only (no switching-level verification, DCM, dead time, sensing delay);
simplified loss model; synthetic battery and profiles; seconds-long horizons so SOC behaviour is
shown by initial conditions; identical shading across strings; coarse tuning grid with optima on
its edge; a reliance on load-current feed-forward for tight bus regulation; no Simulink /
OpenModelica cross-check and no hardware validation. Natural extensions: a switched model of
the boost stage to verify ripple and loop margins, a quasi-static day-long EMS simulation with
measured irradiance, noise-aware variants of dP-P&O, and a tuned or event-scheduled global scan.
